title.narrative: Restore access to quality health services to local communities living in the areas most affected by Hurricane Oscar

description.narrative: The damage to the health sector following the impact of Hurricane Oscar includes damage to infrastructure, mainly roofing, as well as the loss of medical and dental equipment, medical devises and supplies for institutions and entities. One component of the event that aggravated the situation was the slow speed of 4km/h and the accumulated water of 300 millimeters in 24 hours, which caused the rivers in the area to swell and the subsequent flooding of low-lying areas, including health centers, affecting healthcare equipment. In addition, the national electro-energy system collapsed, making it impossible to provide proper early warning and make timely decisions in many of the affected areas. This situation also complicates their immediate recovery and the vitality of services. Initial reports indicate damage to 56 health institutions, among them the General Hospital: Octavio de la Concepción y Pedraza in Baracoa, 7 polyclinics and 38 family doctors' offices and Nurse Clinics (CMF), as well as 5 pharmacies. Eight deaths have been reported in Guantánamo, but this figure is expected to rise due to the unprecedented flooding. The Maternal and Infant Care Programme also requires medicines, supplies, sexual and reproductive health kits, hygiene kits, bedding and pregnant women's clothes for maternity homes, shock-proof suits for transporting critical mothers, and vitamin supplements for pregnant women and postpartum women. Information on the damage caused by Hurricane Oscar is still preliminary, as the assessment of damages and needs has not yet been completed, mainly due to the lack of communication with the municipalities. In the particular case of the municipality of Imías, there is still flooding in the area of Los Pinos and in the local "Ciro Frías Cabrera" polyclinic (stable communication has not been achieved, so it has not been possible to quantify all the damages and losses). Hurricane Oscar occur in a complex epidemiological context, with co-circulation of dengue, oropouche and various respiratory viruses, which could increase in the post-Hurricane conditions while other communicable diseases such as leptospirosis and water-borne diseases could also appear as a result of the floods. Added to the current context of energy crisis in the country, the risks are accentuated by the inability of the health system to respond promptly and efficiently enough to deal with disease outbreaks.This CERF project will support the recovery of the operational capacity of the 8 most affected health institutions - 1 hospital in Baracoa and 7 polyclinics - in the four impacted municipalities to provide essential health services in safe sanitary conditions as well as quickly identify and attend health risks faced by vulnerable populations living in affected areas, including mental health affectations as well as risks of communicable disease outbreaks. Funds will be used to procure and deliver essential relief items as well as medicines and medical supplies and equipment to affected health institutions to restore operations and support continued care delivery capacity to people living in affected municipalities. PAHO/WHO will also support the intensification of epidemiological surveillance and vector control capacity to ensure the timely detection of disease outbreaks, particularly of water-borne and vector-borne diseases in the current context of deteriorated WASH conditions as well as active circulation of infectious pathogens. Activities will focus on the procurement of supplies and equipment, as well as rapid training of health personnel.
